newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook - March stragglers weigh heavy.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook - March stragglers weigh heavy.

text.p: A raft of unsold March North Sea barrels and a rising tide of Iraqi exports will dash any hopes sellers may have harboured for firmer European spot crude differentials this week, traders said.

Ample supply of Dated Brent and stragglers from the March Norwegian programmes, coupled with lower prices for Kirkuk Blend sales to Europe, will outweigh the positive impact of thinner April supply and a slight improvement in refining margins.
"Fundamentally the Brent market is the worst I've seen for a long time and there are other grades available as well," said a senior trader for a European major.

As many as seven Brent cargoes due to load in the last week of March were still unsold on Monday and there was little prospect of sales to the United States given a narrow NYMEX premium over Brent crude futures.
High freight rates for very large crude carriers (VLCCs) also limited traders' options.
"These cargoes are a problem. Something needs to move out of the region but nothing works and anyway there is no buying out there," said the trader.
Brent was offered into the U.S. Gulf last week at about WTI less 50 cents but bids were seen at least 30 cents below that.

Dated Brent, which saw its April paper-related value lose 40 cents last week, was expected to slide further despite better cracking margins and April loading programmes showing North Sea supply would fall by about 60,000 barrels per day (bpd).
A Brent cargo loading March 26-28 traded on Friday at April Brent less 71 cents a barrel on Friday.

"The market has already reacted to the programmes which is why we're about $1.50 off the low (on Brent futures), but there's still quite a lot of prompt oil about which is hitting differentials," said a trader.
"All these things have picked up and normally they would help but given the volume of crude which is hanging around I don't see it improving," said another trader.
Mediterranean sour crudes also looked set for further losses, given the U.N.'s approval of bigger discounts for sales of Iraqi Kirkuk Blend crude into Europe.
Kirkuk would be priced at Dated Brent less $1.80 from March 10 and Dated Brent less $1.90 for April, a cut of 25 cents.
Lower prices could mean Baghdad has to sell more to meet its $1 billion target for the second 90 days of the oil-food deal.
By contrast, West African markets appeared to have found a floor after sliding dramtically in the last couple of weeks.
Lifters of Nigerian crudes lost heavily as spot values tumbled below the Official Selling Prices (OSPs) set by state Nigerian National Petroleum Corp (NNPC).
Some traders said the March overhang of Nigerian barrels had dwindled to around three million barrels and early April sales to the Far East were helping to provide support.
Others only saw temporary relief with Asian demand expected to dwindle as refineries enter a heavy programme of maintenance.
